question: What is the main job of the systemic circulation?

options.A: Producing red blood cells within bone marrow
options.B: Pumping blood directly into the alveoli
options.C: Supplying oxygenated blood to body tissues
options.D: Filtering waste products inside the kidneys

explanation: You've got this! The systemic circulation acts like a dedicated delivery service, carrying oxygen and vital nutrients from the heart to every single organ and tissue in the body. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h1)

question: How is the systemic circulation different from the pulmonary circulation?

options.A: It carries deoxygenated blood inside arteries
options.B: It operates under much lower blood pressure
options.C: It serves body tissues instead of the lungs
options.D: It bypasses the right side of the heart

explanation: Think of it this way: the pulmonary circuit runs to the lungs to pick up oxygen, while the systemic circuit takes that freshly oxygenated blood and shares it with the rest of the body! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h1)

question: Which chamber of the heart pumps blood straight into the aorta?
explanation: Great job remembering your heart anatomy! The left ventricle has thick, muscular walls because it needs enough power to push blood out through the aortic valve and into the aorta. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h2)

question: Where does blood go right after it passes through the aortic valve?

options.B: It collects inside the right atrium
options.C: It drains into the superior vena cava
options.D: It flows into the pulmonary veins

explanation: Spot on! The aortic valve sits right at the exit of the left ventricle, opening up to let blood flow straight into the ascending aorta. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h2)

question: Which blood vessels act like tiny control taps to regulate local blood flow?
explanation: Think of arterioles as the body's plumbing valves. Their muscular walls can tighten or relax to control exactly how much blood flows into the tiny capillary beds. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h3)

question: If a patient's arterioles suddenly narrow all over the body, what happens to their blood pressure right away?

options.B: Blood pressure fluctuates only in veins

explanation: Makes total sense when you picture it: if you narrow the pipes (increasing resistance), the pressure inside them has to go up! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h3)

question: What special structural feature makes capillaries so good at exchanging substances with tissues?

options.B: Multiple layers of fibrous connective tissue

explanation: Capillaries are built for business! Because their walls are only one cell thick, gases, nutrients, and waste products can slip across them with ease. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h4)

question: Which force pushes fluid out of the capillary and into the surrounding tissues?
explanation: You've got this! Hydrostatic pressure is simply the push of blood pressure inside the vessel, forcing fluid out into the tissues where it's needed. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h4)

question: What keeps blood from flowing backward in medium-sized veins?
explanation: Exactly! Veins have clever little one-way valves that snap shut to make sure blood only moves forward toward the heart, fighting against gravity. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h5)

question: What helps push venous blood all the way from your legs back up to your heart?
explanation: Every time you walk or move your legs, your skeletal muscles squeeze the deep veins like a tube of toothpaste, pumping blood upward toward the heart! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h5)

question: Which factor has the biggest impact on systemic vascular resistance?
explanation: Think about a garden hose: even a tiny change in the width of the opening makes a huge difference in how hard the water pushes against the sides. Same goes for blood vessels! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h6)

question: What does mean arterial pressure (MAP) actually tell us?

options.A: Total volume of blood pumped per minute
options.B: Average driving pressure in systemic vessels
options.C: Peak pressure generated by the left ventricle

explanation: MAP is your overall gauge. It represents the average pressure pushing blood through your organs to keep them happy and alive throughout the entire cardiac cycle. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h6)

question: Which clinical sign usually tells you that a patient has poor peripheral tissue perfusion?
explanation: When the body is low on perfusion, it panics and saves blood for the vital organs (heart and brain). That leaves the fingers and toes feeling cool and looking pale. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h7)

question: If a patient's capillary refill time is sluggish and takes five seconds, what does that suggest?
explanation: Normal refill is under two seconds. If it takes five seconds, blood is having a hard time traveling through those tiny vessels in the skin due to poor circulation. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h7)

question: What waste product builds up when tissues don't get enough oxygen because of poor circulation?
explanation: When cells are starved of oxygen, they panic and switch to backup energy production (anaerobic metabolism), which unfortunately leaves behind lactic acid as a waste byproduct. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h8)

question: Which organ is often the first to show trouble when systemic blood flow drops significantly?
explanation: Kidneys are very sensitive divas when it comes to blood flow! If systemic pressure drops, they quickly show it by cutting back on urine production. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h8)
